bills.title: Kids Online Safety Act
bills.official_title: A bill to protect the safety of children on the internet.
bills.summary: The Kids Online Safety Act puts a legal duty on social platforms, online video games, messaging apps, and video streaming services that minors are likely to use: they must take reasonable care in how they design features so those features do not push minors toward a listed set of harms, and they must give minors and parents built-in safety controls that start on the most protective setting. Platforms averaging more than 10,000,000 monthly U.S. users would also have to publish a yearly report based on an outside audit, and a separate title would require any online platform using a personalized ranking algorithm to let users switch to one that does not use data about them.
bills.brief: Creates a federal duty of care over how covered platforms design features that affect minors, plus default-on safeguards, parental tools, audited annual transparency reports for the largest platforms, and an opt-out from personalized ranking algorithms.

top_lines.headline: Duty of Care Over Design Features
subs: Reasonable care in creating design features to prevent seven listed harms
Covers compulsive usage, sexual exploitation, and financial harms
Does not require blocking content a minor independently searches for

top_lines.headline: Default Safeguards and Parental Tools
subs: Safeguards default to the most protective setting for known minors
Reports on harm answered in 10 days above 10,000,000 monthly users
No advertising of drugs, tobacco, cannabis, gambling, or alcohol to minors

top_lines.headline: Audits, Enforcement, and Algorithm Opt-Out
subs: Annual third-party audited public report for the largest platforms
FTC enforces; State attorneys general limited to sections 103 to 105
Users may switch to a ranking algorithm using no user-specific data

bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by a Republican in a Republican-majority Senate and carrying 76 cosponsors split 42 R, 33 D and 1 I — a cosponsor count above the 60-vote cloture threshold and split roughly evenly by party, which is the strongest structural signal in this bill's favor. The Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee has ordered it reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, per the latest-action metadata; that substitute text is not published on Congress.gov, so this analysis describes the introduced text. Opposition is likeliest over the duty of care in section 102, which the bill answers with an express First Amendment viewpoint limit and a carve-out for content a minor independently seeks, and over the compliance cost of the annual third-party audit; the House would still have to take up a companion.

items.main: Requires a covered platform to exercise reasonable care in the creation and implementation of any design feature to prevent and mitigate seven categories of harm to minors, limited to harms a reasonable and prudent person would agree were reasonably foreseeable and to which the design feature is a contributing factor.
items.detail: The listed harms are eating disorders, substance use disorders and suicidal behaviors; depressive and anxiety disorders with objectively verifiable and clinically diagnosable symptoms that are related to compulsive usage; patterns of use indicating compulsive usage; physical violence or online harassment severe, pervasive, or objectively offensive enough to affect a major life activity; sexual exploitation and abuse of minors; distribution, sale, or use of narcotic drugs, tobacco, cannabis, gambling, or alcohol; and financial harms from unfair or deceptive acts or practices. The duty does not require a platform to stop a minor from deliberately and independently searching for content or from reaching resources about preventing those harms, and no government entity may enforce it based on the viewpoint of users expressed through speech protected by the First Amendment.

items.main: Defines the regulated class as covered platforms — online platforms, online video games, messaging applications, and video streaming services used or reasonably likely to be used by a minor — with a minor being under 17 and a child under 13.
items.detail: The definition excludes common carrier services, broadband internet access service, email, teleconferencing or video conferencing meeting stated conditions, standalone wireless messaging services, non-profit organizations, schools from preschool through higher education, libraries, news or sports coverage sites where video relates to their own reporting, business-to-business software, virtual private networks, and government entities with a .gov domain. A design feature is any feature or component that will encourage or increase the frequency, time spent, or activity of minors, including infinite scrolling, auto play, notifications, badges, in-game purchases, and appearance altering filters.

items.main: Requires readily accessible safeguards for users the platform knows are minors — limiting who can contact them, restricting public access to their personal data, limiting engagement-increasing design features by default, controlling personalized recommendation systems, and restricting geolocation sharing — with the default set to the most protective level the platform offers unless a parent changes it.
items.detail: Minors must get a prominently displayed option to opt out of personalized recommendation systems while still seeing content in a chronological format, an option to limit recommendation categories, and an option to limit time spent. Parental tools must let a parent view privacy and account settings, change them for a known child, restrict purchases and financial transactions, and view and restrict total time spent; those tools are enabled by default for known children, and the platform must give the minor clear and conspicuous notice when they are in effect.

items.main: Requires an easy reporting route for harms to a minor with a substantive response within 10 days for platforms averaging more than 10,000,000 monthly active U.S. users, 21 days for smaller platforms, and as promptly as needed where the report involves an imminent threat.
items.detail: The section also makes it unlawful to design or manipulate a user interface with the purpose or substantial effect of obscuring, subverting, or impairing user choice over these safeguards or parental tools, and bars a covered platform from facilitating advertising of narcotic drugs, cannabis products, tobacco products, gambling, or alcohol to an individual it knows is a minor. Online video games need not interrupt the natural sequence of gameplay to apply these controls, and changes made while a device is offline apply the next time it connects.

items.main: Requires a covered platform that averaged more than 10,000,000 monthly active U.S. users in the most recent calendar year and predominantly provides a community forum for user-generated content to publish, at least annually, a report based on an independent third-party audit conducted with a reasonable level of assurance.
items.detail: The report must assess how likely the platform is to be accessed by minors, describe the commercial interests being served by minors' use, and account for the number of known minor users, the median and mean time they spend daily, weekly and monthly, the content they access in English and the top 5 non-English languages, and the reports received through the section 103 mechanism disaggregated by those languages. It must also evaluate the efficacy of the safeguards and parental tools and describe mitigation measures taken. The platform must give the auditor all relevant information, materials, and system access, and must present data in de-identified aggregated form.

sections.label: Section 202 — Requirement To Allow Users To See Unmanipulated Content on Internet Platforms

items.main: Makes it unlawful, beginning 1 year after enactment, to operate an online platform using an opaque algorithm unless the operator discloses how it works and lets users easily switch to an input-transparent algorithm.
items.detail: An opaque algorithm ranks content based in whole or part on user-specific data the user did not expressly provide for that purpose; an input-transparent algorithm uses only data the user did supply, such as search terms, filters, saved preferences, followed accounts, and current precise or approximate geolocation — precise meaning within a range of 5 miles or less. Required notices cover the algorithm's most salient features, inputs and parameters, how user-specific data is collected or inferred, available opt-out options, and the quantities the algorithm is designed to optimize. Platforms may not deny service, change prices, or condition service on a user's choice of the input-transparent option, and need not disclose trade secrets, confidential business information, or privileged material.

underreported.section: Section 109(b)(6) — Enforcement by State Attorneys General
underreported.summary: State attorneys general may bring civil actions only for violations of sections 103, 104, and 105, and a violation of the section 102 duty of care may not form the basis of liability in any action a State attorney general brings under a State law.
underreported.why_unreported: Section 102 carries the bill's central obligation, and the enforcement section places it outside the State-level route available for the other duties, leaving it to the Federal Trade Commission.

underreported.summary: Nothing in the title, including the determination of whether a platform has knowledge fairly implied on the basis of objective circumstances, may be construed to require a platform to collect age data it is not already collecting or to implement age gating or age verification functionality.
underreported.why_unreported: The title's duties attach to users a platform knows are minors, and this provision means the knowledge standard cannot itself be read to require the age-checking that would establish that knowledge.

underreported.section: Section 112(e) — Application to Video Streaming Services
underreported.summary: A video streaming service is deemed in compliance with the entire title if its content is predominantly preselected by the provider rather than user-generated, any interactive functionality is incidental, and — unless it is predominantly news or sports — it can limit minors' access, limit autoplay of recommended content, offer parental settings and purchase restrictions, provide a point of contact and a notice, and avoid serving the listed advertising categories to known minors.
underreported.why_unreported: Video streaming services are named in the covered platform definition, and this subsection sets a separate checklist under which they satisfy the title without applying sections 102 through 105 as written.

underreported.section: Section 108(c) — Limitation on Federal Trade Commission Guidance
underreported.summary: The guidance the Commission must issue confers no rights and binds no person, State, locality, court, or the Commission itself, and an enforcement action may not be based on practices alleged only to be inconsistent with that guidance.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill requires two guidance documents within 18 months, including one on how the Commission would apply the knowledge standard, while providing that neither can supply the basis for an enforcement action.

gaps: The definition of geolocation in section 101 takes its meaning from a Children's Online Privacy Protection Act definition described as added by section 201(a), but section 201 of the bill is a flat list of definitions for title II with no subsection (a) and makes no amendment to that Act.

Section 110 sets the Kids Online Safety Council at 11 members with a fixed allocation among the President and four congressional leaders, and separately requires 1 member from each of 9 listed categories, without stating how the appointment allocation and the category requirement are reconciled.

The bill requires safeguards, parental tools, and default settings for users a platform knows are minors, but expressly does not require any age verification or age gating and does not otherwise specify how a platform is to identify which users are minors.

The transparency reports must be based on an independent third-party audit, but the bill sets no auditor qualification, independence, accreditation, or conflict-of-interest standard, and leaves technical standards for audits to the recommendations of a Council whose final report is due 3 years after its first meeting.

The duty of care and the safeguards apply to covered platforms reasonably likely to be used by a minor, but the title takes effect 18 months after enactment while the section 108 guidance interpreting the design-feature and knowledge standards is also due at 18 months, so the guidance is not due before the duties attach.

added: A duty of care requiring covered platforms to exercise reasonable care in creating and implementing design features to prevent and mitigate seven listed categories of harm to minors

Required safeguards for known minors covering communication limits, personal data visibility, engagement-increasing design features, personalized recommendation controls, geolocation sharing, and time spent, defaulting to the most protective level offered
Parental tools for known minors, enabled by default for known children, covering privacy and account settings, purchase restrictions, and time spent

A reporting mechanism for harms to a minor with substantive-response deadlines of 10 days for platforms above 10,000,000 monthly active U.S. users and 21 days below that, and as promptly as needed for imminent threats
A prohibition on facilitating advertising of narcotic drugs, cannabis products, tobacco products, gambling, or alcohol to a user the platform knows is a minor
An annual public transparency report based on an independent third-party audit for the largest community-forum platforms
A bar on market or product-focused research on a known child, and on a known minor without verifiable parental consent

An 11-member Kids Online Safety Council, appointed within 180 days of enactment, reporting to Congress 1 year and 3 years after its initial meeting and terminating within 30 days of that final report, and not subject to the Federal Advisory Committee Act

A requirement, beginning 1 year after enactment, that an online platform using an opaque algorithm give notice of how it works and let users easily switch to an input-transparent algorithm, with no differential pricing for that choice
A study by the Secretary of Commerce with the Federal Communications Commission and the Federal Trade Commission on device-level and operating-system-level age verification, reported within 1 year
modified: A violation of title I or of section 202 is treated as a violation of a rule defining an unfair or deceptive act or practice under section 18(a)(1)(B) of the Federal Trade Commission Act, enforced with the Commission's existing powers
State attorneys general gain parens patriae civil actions for violations of sections 103, 104, and 105, with notice to the Commission and a Commission right to intervene and remove
